decisionMemo.businessProblem: A mature, profitable $85M-revenue industrial equipment manufacturer (~$11M EBITDA, higher-margin ~30% aftermarket stream) is owned ~100% by a 64-year-old founder who wants a fair liquidity event and an orderly exit within ~18-24 months while protecting ~310 employees and a 40-year reputation. There is no internal successor and value is concentrated in the founder and 2-3 long-tenured leaders, with top-5 customer concentration at ~38%. He must choose among (A) a financial/PE buyer (faster, EBITDA-multiple-based, often requiring an earn-out or management retention he cannot personally provide), (B) a strategic buyer (potential synergy premium but integration/relocation risk and harder to source), or (C) retaining and running for cash flow with hired management (preserves control/reputation but defers liquidity and concentrates wealth in an illiquid, key-person-dependent asset). The business's transferable value, aftermarket durability, and key-person dependence are not yet substantiated to buyer-diligence standard, and any path that requires the founder's continued daily leadership past ~24 months is unacceptable.

rootCauseDiagnosis.description: Loss of market position due to brand/reputation damage
rootCauseDiagnosis.mechanismDescription: Customer perception of brand has shifted negative. Market position erodes as customers perceive competitors as superior or more trustworthy. Premium positioning collapses.
alternativeExplanations: Actual product quality declined (not perception issue)
Competitive product innovation may be superior
missingEvidenceFor: Customer perception data vs actual quality

factors.rationale: Expected revenue impact: MINOR. Urgency: MEDIUM-HIGH (no operational crisis, but the founder's age, lack of successor, and key-person concentration make an orderly transition time-sensitive; a poorly prepared process risks a discounted outcome and workforce/reputation harm)

recommendedInterventions.sequencingReason: Quick implementation builds momentum and shows progress

scenarios.name: Aggressive Recovery (Best Case)
scenarios.description: Execute all interventions in optimal sequence with full team commitment
assumptions: Team capacity fully available (no other initiatives)
Client budget approved for all recommended interventions
No external market shocks during implementation
scenarios.expectedOutcome: Revenue recovery within 90 days, competitive positioning restored
risks: Cascading failures if one intervention stumbles

scenarios.name: Staged Implementation (Recommended)
scenarios.description: Execute top 3 prioritized interventions sequentially, measure, then decide on next wave
assumptions: Top 3 interventions address critical path to revenue recovery
Team capacity for 1-2 major initiatives at a time
Monthly review gates to assess progress and adjust
scenarios.expectedOutcome: Measurable improvement in 60 days, foundation for growth set
risks: Slower overall recovery than aggressive path
Competitors may advance while we execute gradually

limitations: Evidence gaps limit precision: Weak evidence on Customer Retention - diagnosis confidence limited; Critical gap: No evidence on Operational Efficiency
Evidence coverage is insufficient across business dimensions. Deeper investigation recommended before diagnosis finalization.
nextReviewTriggers: After first intervention completion: validate assumptions, collect outcome data
Monthly: Track KPIs (repeat customer rate, turnaround time, complaint count)
If revenue does not improve by 20% within 60 days: pivot to alternative diagnosis
If team capacity exhausted: pause non-critical interventions
If external market changes significantly: reassess competitive positioning
